opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question. So much of the progress we've seen in AI for biology so far has been built on data that's very clean and very structured: protein structures in the PDB, sequence databases, biochemical assay results. Those are fantastic because they're relatively standardized and there's a lot of it, and that's what enabled things like structure prediction to really take off.

But when you think about what actually matters for drug discovery, the real question is what happens when a molecule goes into a living system. Does it reach the right tissue? How is it metabolized? What are the off-target effects across the whole organism, not just against one protein in a test tube? That's the in vivo world, and it's where most drug programs fail. A huge fraction of attrition in the clinic comes from things like toxicity or lack of efficacy that you just couldn't see from the isolated, in vitro picture.

The challenge is that in vivo data is messy. It's expensive to generate, it's lower throughput, it's heterogeneous across labs and protocols, and a lot of it sits in silos inside pharma companies. So it hasn't had its "PDB moment" yet. There isn't one big, well-curated, standardized dataset that everyone can train on.

That's exactly why I think it's such a major open area. If we can build models that bridge from the molecular level, where we're getting really good, up to cellular, tissue, and organism-level behavior, that's where you start to really change the probability of success for a drug. It means thinking hard about how to generate the right data, how to make it consistent enough to learn from, and how to design models that can combine all these different scales and modalities. To me that's one of the biggest frontiers: moving from modeling the parts of biology to modeling the system.

r001.rationale: The response says in vivo data is expensive to generate and lower throughput, identifying limited ability to generate it at scale as a constraint.

fable-5.1.text:
Max Jaderberg: So if you think about what a model of biology actually needs to capture, it's not just how a protein folds or how a molecule binds to a target. That's the part we've gotten really good at. AlphaFold-style models, structure prediction, binding affinity — those operate at a scale where the physics is relatively clean and the data is relatively abundant. But the thing we ultimately care about in drug discovery is what happens in a whole organism. Does this molecule actually make a patient better? Is it toxic? Does it get where it needs to go? And that's an in vivo question.

The reason I think of it as a major open area is that almost all the data we train on today is in vitro. It's cell lines in a dish, it's biochemical assays, it's very controlled systems that we've engineered precisely so we can measure them reproducibly. And those are fantastic for building models, but they're a simplified proxy. The actual organism is this incredibly complex, multi-scale, dynamic system — tissues, immune responses, metabolism, feedback loops — and the gap between what works in a dish and what works in a mouse, let alone a human, is enormous. That gap is basically where most drugs fail.

So the question becomes: can we start to learn models that bridge that gap? And to do that, you need in vivo data at scale, and you need it structured in a way machine learning can actually consume. Right now in vivo data is sparse, it's expensive, it's noisy, it's often locked away in individual labs or pharma companies in formats that don't compose. There's no equivalent of the PDB for in vivo outcomes. So part of the opportunity is on the data generation side — thinking about how you design experiments where the output is a signal a model can learn from, rather than a single endpoint read out by a human.

And the other part is the modeling itself. We've seen that when you have the right data, these models generalize in ways that surprise you. I think the same thing will be true of whole-organism biology. Nobody's really pushed on that yet, because the data hasn't been there. But if we can close the loop — model makes a prediction, you run the in vivo experiment, you feed the result back — that's where I think the really big wins are going to come from. It's the part of the problem that actually determines whether a medicine reaches a patient, and it's almost entirely untouched by modern AI.

r001.rationale: The response says in vivo data is needed at scale and describes it as sparse, expensive, and difficult to combine, identifying data availability and generation as constraints on modeling.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the gap between what we can measure in a relatively controlled experiment and what we ultimately care about, which is what happens in a living organism. You can learn something about a molecule or a cell in isolation, but in vivo you’ve got all these systems interacting. Does a drug get to the right tissue? What does it do there? How does the rest of the organism respond?

That’s an incredibly rich modeling problem, but it’s also a data problem. The experiments are harder to run, the measurements are more complex, and you don’t necessarily get the scale or consistency that you’d like for training models.

So the opportunity is to build that connection between better experiments and better models. Can you collect in vivo data that helps you predict what an intervention will actually do, and then use the model to choose the next experiment? If you can get that loop working, you start to close the gap between understanding biology in a simplified setting and making something that works in the body.

r001.rationale: The response says in vivo experiments are harder and that their scale may fall short of what is needed to train models, identifying limited data scale as a constraint.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the progress in applying AI to biology has come from systems where we can generate large amounts of relatively controlled data. But biology ultimately happens in a living organism, where you have all these interacting systems—the immune system, metabolism, different tissues—and that context can completely change what a molecule does.

So there’s a really important gap between being able to predict an effect in a cell assay and understanding whether an intervention will actually work in an organism. In vivo data gives you a window into that, but it’s much harder to collect at scale, and it’s more heterogeneous and difficult to interpret.

That makes it a major opportunity: how do you build models that learn from those complex measurements, connect them to what we know at the molecular and cellular levels, and help choose the next experiment? It’s not just a question of making a bigger model. It’s also about figuring out how to generate the right data so that the model can learn something useful about biology in its full context.

r001.rationale: The response says in vivo data is much harder to collect at scale, identifying limited scalability as a constraint on modeling.
